Chapter Three: The Trap of Survivorship Bias—Why Most Success Stories Mislead
Everywhere you look, it feels like you’re surrounded by stories of winners. There’s the entrepreneur who started from nothing and built an empire, the athlete who beat the odds, or the investor who struck it rich. These stories are inspiring—no doubt. But here’s what we often forget: for every one of these headline-makers, there are countless others who tried, struggled, and quietly faded away, their stories lost to time.
This is what’s known as survivorship bias. It’s our natural tendency to focus on those who made it while overlooking those who didn’t. And it’s sneaky—shaping the way we see the world, and what we believe is possible. Take the world of finance, for example. Magazines are filled with profiles of top fund managers. Books dive deep into their strategies. Investors scramble to copy what worked for them. But here’s the catch: for every celebrated winner, there are far more who took the same risks and lost everything.
Imagine a group of old friends at a reunion, sharing stories about their careers. One beams about a big promotion, another about a successful startup. The mood is upbeat, hopeful. But nobody talks about the failed ventures, the layoffs, or the dreams that didn’t pan out. The stories we hear are the ones with happy endings, which creates a skewed picture of reality.
When we focus only on the winners, we start making some risky assumptions. We convince ourselves that success is simply about hard work and determination. We ignore the role of luck, the impact of timing, and all those unpredictable factors that can change everything. The odds of success get blown out of proportion, and the very real risks start to fade from view.
In the world of investing, this bias can get expensive—fast. Investors pile into the hottest funds, convinced that past performance means future results. But what they don’t see are all the funds that started at the same time and quietly disappeared. The winners are celebrated, the losers are forgotten, and the cycle just keeps repeating.
Picture a young analyst, eager to make her mark. She studies the top traders, copies their strategies, and hopes to match their success. What she doesn’t realize is that so many others tried the exact same thing—and failed. The stories she’s reading? They’re just the visible survivors floating above a sea of invisible failures.
Now, recognizing survivorship bias doesn’t mean you should give up on your goals. It’s about seeing the world with a clearer lens—understanding the real odds, and making smarter decisions. When you look beyond just the winners and consider all the outcomes, you can sidestep the trap of false hope and misplaced confidence.
So, next time you hear a success story, remember: it’s just the tip of the iceberg. There’s always more beneath the surface.
